title: Synthetic data and model collapse
summary: Why models trained recursively on their own outputs lose the tails and collapse, what the math says about replacing versus accumulating data, and how filtered, diverse synthetic data is used safely.
outcomes: Explain why finite resampling erases rare events and why a fully synthetic loop is absorbed into a point mass
Compute the per-generation chance of losing a token and the variance drift of a Gaussian fit-and-resample loop
Explain how temperature, top-k and top-p cut tails and why that makes scaling plateau
Compare replace and accumulate loops and compute their test error in the linear regression model
Design a synthetic data pipeline with outside filtering, injected diversity and real-data anchoring

lessons.title: Why resampling your own outputs erases rare events

blocks.md: From the training course you know an LLM is pretrained on a huge web scrape, then fine-tuned. Two things now put model-written text into that pipeline. Labs generate **synthetic data** on purpose (instructions, reasoning traces, textbook-style explanations), and the web itself fills with model output that a future scrape will collect. Either way, a model can end up learning from the outputs of earlier models.

Shumailov et al. asked what happens when this repeats: model 1 is trained on real data, model 2 on samples from model 1, model 3 on samples from model 2, and so on. They named the result **model collapse**: a degenerative process where each generation's output pollutes the next generation's training set, so models slowly forget the true distribution. They separate **early collapse**, where the rare events in the tails of the distribution vanish, from **late collapse**, where the model converges to a distribution with little resemblance to the original, often with much smaller variance.

Start with the simplest possible model: no neural network at all. The "model" is a histogram over 6 tokens, fitted by counting. Each generation draws $M = 20$ samples from the current histogram, counts them, and the new counts divided by 20 become the next model. Fitting is perfect here; the only error is that 20 samples are a finite sample. The true probabilities are 0.40, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, 0.07 and 0.03.

blocks.prompt: The rarest token, *aardvark*, has probability 0.03. With 20 samples per generation, what is the chance that generation 1 contains no aardvark at all?
blocks.reveal: About **54%**. The chance one sample misses it is 0.97, so all 20 miss with probability $0.97^{20} = 0.544$. Its expected count is $20 \times 0.03 = 0.6$, less than one occurrence. Once a count is zero, the fitted histogram gives that token probability zero, so it can never be sampled again.

blocks.tex: P(\text{token lost in one generation}) = (1-q)^M, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\text{count}] = Mq
blocks.caption: q is the token's current probability, M the samples per generation. Any token with q below 1/M is expected to appear less than once.

blocks.title: One run of the fit-and-resample loop (M = 20)

scenes.caption: Generation 0 is the real distribution. aardvark (0.03) and mat (0.07) both have expected counts below 1.5 in a sample of 20.
Generation 1: mat drew zero samples and is gone for good. Sampling noise also inflated on from 0.10 to 0.25 and gave aardvark one lucky sample.
Generation 3: sat (true probability 0.15) also drew zero. Loss is random, not strictly rarest first, but rare tokens are lost most often.
Generation 6: aardvark is lost. Half of the original vocabulary is now unreachable, while on has drifted up to 0.50.
Generation 19: on is lost. Only two tokens remain, and the estimates wander freely because nothing anchors them to the truth.
Generation 22: every sample is the. The histogram is a single spike and resampling it reproduces it forever. This is late collapse.

blocks.md: Why must every run end in a spike? The sequence of histograms is a **Markov chain**: the next histogram depends only on the current one. A histogram with all mass on one token reproduces itself exactly, so it is an **absorbing state**, and a chain that can reach an absorbing state from anywhere is absorbed with probability 1. Shumailov et al. also note the chance of ending on a given token equals its original probability. In 20,000 simulated runs of this example, *the* won 39.6% of the time (true 0.40) and *aardvark* 2.9% (true 0.03), and the mean time to a single spike was 32.5 generations.
In a closed loop that only ever trains on its own samples, information can be lost but never regained. Rare events go first, because their expected count in a finite sample is below one.

Model collapse is not caused by a bad model or a bug. In this example fitting is exact. The finite sample alone, which Shumailov et al. call **statistical approximation error**, is enough to drive the process.

blocks.question: A token's fitted probability hits exactly 0 at generation 4 of this fully synthetic loop. What is the chance it reappears at generation 50?
options: About its original probability, because errors average out over generations
Small but positive, because sampling is random
Zero, because a token with probability 0 is never sampled and refitting cannot invent it
About 1/M, because each generation draws M fresh samples
blocks.explain: The histogram model can only assign mass to tokens it has seen. Once a count is zero the token has probability zero, so no later sample contains it. Only an outside source of real data could bring it back.

blocks.question: In the absorbing chain above, cat starts at probability 0.25. Over many independent runs, roughly how often does cat end up as the sole surviving token?
options: About 25% of runs
Never, only the most common token can win
About 1/6 of runs, since all tokens are symmetric
About 50%, since it is the second most likely
blocks.explain: The fitted probability is a martingale: its expected value never changes, so the chance of absorbing at a token equals its starting probability. The 20,000-run simulation gave 25.5% for cat.

lessons.title: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point

blocks.md: The histogram had discrete tokens. Real models fit continuous distributions, so take the next simplest case. The data are one-dimensional Gaussian, $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$. Each generation draws $M$ samples from the current model, then fits a new Gaussian using the **unbiased** sample mean and sample variance (dividing by $M-1$). The next generation samples from that fit.

blocks.caption: The recursive fitting process from Shumailov et al. (Eq. 1 and 2 of the arXiv version).

blocks.title: Fit, sample, refit: one seeded run with M = 10
blocks.code:
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
mu, sigma, M = 0.0, 1.0, 10
for gen in range(1, 101):
    x = rng.normal(mu, sigma, M)  # sample from current model
    mu = x.mean()                 # refit the mean
    sigma = x.std(ddof=1)         # refit with unbiased variance
print(round(mu, 3), round(sigma, 4))

scenes.caption: Generation 0 is the true distribution: mean 0, standard deviation 1. Only 10 samples are drawn per generation.
After one fit the estimate is already off: the 10 samples happened to be bunched together, so sigma dropped to 0.781.
Generation 10: sigma is 0.430. Each fit starts from the previous fit, not from the truth, so errors compound instead of cancelling.
Generation 50: sigma is 0.104 and the mean has wandered to -0.374. The model now covers only a sliver around a wrong center.
Generation 100: sigma is about 0.0001. Late collapse: a near point mass at a random location. The mean has stopped moving because the steps scale with sigma.

blocks.prompt: The variance estimator is unbiased: averaged over runs, $\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_{n+1}] = \sigma^2_n$, so $\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2_n] = 1$ at every generation. How can almost every run still collapse toward zero?
blocks.reveal: Because the average is carried by rare runs. The product of many random factors with mean 1 is typically far below 1: each generation multiplies $\sigma^2$ by a factor $S$ whose mean is 1 but whose log has a negative mean. In 200,000 simulated runs with $M = 10$, at generation 10 the average $\sigma^2$ was 1.006, yet the median $\sigma$ was 0.573 and 43% of runs had $\sigma < 0.5$. A few runs with huge variance hold the average up while the typical run shrinks.

blocks.md: Write the update as $\sigma^2_{n+1} = \sigma^2_n S_n$, where $S_n = \chi^2_{M-1}/(M-1)$ is an independent random factor with mean exactly 1 (a chi-squared variable with $M-1$ degrees of freedom is a sum of $M-1$ squared standard normals, divided here by its mean). Taking logs turns the product into a sum: $\ln \sigma^2_n = \sum_i \ln S_i$. By Jensen's inequality $\mathbb{E}[\ln S] < \ln \mathbb{E}[S] = 0$, so the log-variance is a random walk with a downward drift, and the law of large numbers drives it to minus infinity.

blocks.caption: psi is the digamma function. For M = 10 the exact drift is -0.1152 per generation (the approximation gives -0.1111), so a typical sigma halves about every 12 generations.

scenes.caption: M = 10: sigma halves about every 12 generations and is effectively zero by generation 100. Simplified: this is the drift approximation, not one run.
M = 100: the exact halving time is about 137 generations. Collapse is slower, not prevented.
M = 1000: about 1384 generations per halving. Larger samples only stretch the timeline; Theorem 3.1 of the Nature paper says sigma still goes to 0 almost surely for any fixed M.

blocks.md: Shumailov et al. also measure the distance from the truth with the **Wasserstein-2 distance**, which for two Gaussians is $(\mu_n - \mu)^2 + (\sigma_n - \sigma)^2$ in one dimension. To first order in $1/M$, after $n$ fits its expected value grows linearly: $\mathbb{E}[W_2^2] \approx \tfrac{3}{2}\sigma^2 n/M$ (our simulation with $M = 10$ gave 1.49 at $n = 10$, against 1.5 predicted). The mean takes a random step each generation whose expected squared size stays $\sigma^2/M$ on average (rare high-variance runs keep it up), so the expected error keeps growing even though a typical run's mean freezes as its sigma shrinks, and the paper's Theorem 3.1 states that $\mathbb{E}[W_2^2] \to \infty$ while $\Sigma_n \to 0$ almost surely. Keeping the error bounded would need sample sizes that grow superlinearly with the generation count.

The Nature version lists three error sources that compound over generations: **statistical approximation error** (finite samples, the primary cause), **functional expressivity error** (the model family cannot represent the true distribution, such as fitting one Gaussian to two bumps), and **functional approximation error** (limits of the learning procedure itself, such as biases of SGD or the choice of objective). Real neural networks have all three.
Sampling error makes each generation's fit a random step, and steps that multiply variance by a mean-one factor still shrink it in the typical run. Unbiased estimation does not save a closed loop.

blocks.question: A team fixes collapse in this Gaussian loop by raising M from 10 to 100 samples per generation, keeping everything else the same. What actually happens?
options: Collapse stops, because the estimator becomes accurate enough
Collapse is slowed roughly tenfold (halving time about 12 to about 137 generations) but still happens
Collapse speeds up, because more samples overfit
Nothing changes, because the estimator was already unbiased
blocks.explain: The drift of log-variance is about -1/(M-1) per generation, so a 10x larger sample makes it about 10x smaller. It never reaches zero for finite M, so sigma still tends to 0. Only fresh real data or growing sample sizes change the outcome.

blocks.question: Which statement about the M = 10 loop is correct?
options: The expected variance falls each generation, so the estimator is biased
The typical variance stays near 1, but the expected variance collapses
The expected variance stays at 1, but the typical (median) run collapses toward 0
Both the expected and typical variance stay near 1
blocks.explain: Unbiasedness makes the variance a martingale, so its expectation is 1 forever. The median follows the drift of the log and collapses. A heavy right tail of rare runs keeps the mean at 1.

lessons.title: Language models: decoding cuts the tail, scaling stalls

blocks.md: Does any of this show up in real LLMs? Shumailov et al. fine-tuned Meta's OPT-125m on the wikitext2 dataset, then generated a full synthetic copy of the training set: for every 64-token block of real text, the model continued with 64 tokens using 5-way **beam search**. The next generation was fine-tuned on that synthetic set, and so on. The real-data model reached a mean perplexity of 34 on the wikitext2 test set, down from a zero-shot 115.

Two settings were compared. With no original data kept and 5 epochs per generation, performance degraded over generations. With 10 epochs and a random 10% of the original data kept in every generation, degradation was only minor. Measured by the original model, later generations produced more of the sequences it already found likely, and also a long tail of strange sequences it would never produce. By generation 9 a prompt about church towers produced a list of jackrabbits with differently colored tails.

Language models have an extra way to lose tails that the Gaussian toy lacked: **decoding**. To get fluent synthetic text, practitioners rarely sample from the raw next-token distribution. They use **temperature** $\tau < 1$ (divide logits by $\tau$ before softmax), **top-k** (keep only the $k$ most likely tokens) or **top-p** (keep the smallest set of tokens whose mass reaches $p$). Each one deliberately moves probability away from rare tokens.

blocks.title: One next-token distribution under common decoding settings

scenes.caption: A Zipf-like distribution over 8 tokens: probability proportional to 1/rank. Ranks 5 to 8 hold 23.3% of the mass.
Temperature 0.7: logits divided by 0.7 sharpen the distribution. Ranks 5 to 8 now hold 14.5%.
Temperature 0.5: the tail holds 6.8%. The tail is narrowed, not removed, but rare tokens will appear far less often.
Top-p 0.8 keeps ranks 1 to 5 (cumulative mass 0.84) and renormalizes. Ranks 6 to 8 get exactly zero: they can never appear in the synthetic data.
Top-k 4: only 4 tokens survive. A student model trained on this output has no evidence that ranks 5 to 8 exist.

blocks.md: Dohmatob et al. (*A Tale of Tails*) turn this into a scaling-law statement. Suppose items (facts, skills, token patterns) occur with Zipf frequencies $p_i \propto i^{-\beta}$ with $\beta > 1$, and a model simply memorizes every item it has seen (the "Hutter LLM"). Trained on $T$ real samples, its error falls as $T^{-(\beta-1)/\beta}$. If the training data come from a generator whose tail is cut at rank $k$, items beyond $k$ are never seen, however much data you generate.

blocks.caption: Theorem 2.1 of A Tale of Tails (constants dropped). Once T is larger than about k to the power beta, more synthetic samples stop helping: the error plateaus.

blocks.title: Test error of a memorizing model, real versus tail-cut data (beta = 2)

scenes.caption: Real data: error falls by sqrt(10) per 10x data (exact values 0.0069 at T = 10^4, 0.00069 at 10^6). Simplified: curves follow the shape of Theorem 2.1, fitted to an exact computation over 10 million Zipf items.
Cut at k = 100: the error stalls at 0.00605, exactly the real probability mass beyond rank 100. From T = 10^6 to 10^7 it does not move.
Cut at k = 1000: the plateau drops tenfold and starts later (k squared is 10^6 here). A wider generator tail buys more useful scaling, never unlimited.

blocks.md: Fluency is not coverage. Low temperature and truncation make each synthetic sample look better, and that is exactly why they remove the rare cases a student model needs. The MAD paper finds the same tradeoff for images: biased sampling keeps quality longer but loses diversity faster.

blocks.question: You generate 10x more synthetic training text from the same teacher with top-p 0.9. Under the tail-cutting model, when does this stop improving the student?
options: Never: error keeps falling as a power law in T
Once T exceeds roughly k to the power beta, where k is the effective tail cut; after that error plateaus at the missing tail mass
Immediately: synthetic data never helps
Only when the teacher's perplexity exceeds the student's
blocks.explain: Data from a tail-cut generator only teaches the head of the distribution. Once the student has learned the head, the remaining error is the mass of the items it never sees, and more samples from the same generator cannot reveal them.

blocks.question: In the OPT-125m experiment, which change to the loop gave only minor degradation over generations?
options: Using beam search instead of sampling
Training for fewer epochs
Keeping a random 10% of the original real data in every generation
Generating a synthetic dataset twice as large
blocks.explain: Mixing real data back in each generation re-anchors the model to the true distribution. The paper reports only minor degradation in that setting, versus clear degradation with no original data.

lessons.title: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded

blocks.md: Every loop so far **replaced** the training set each generation: model n saw only model n-1's samples. Gerstgrasser et al. argued that is not how real corpora evolve. Llama 1, 2 and 3 were trained on 1.4, 2 and 15 trillion tokens; data **accumulate**, and synthetic text would be added to, not swapped for, the human text already collected. Alemohammad et al. (the MAD paper) distinguish three loops by how real data enter.

scenes.caption: Fully synthetic loop: after generation 1, each training set is only model output. This is the setting of lessons 1 and 2, and it degrades.
Synthetic augmentation loop: a fixed real set stays in the mix. In MAD's image experiments this only delayed degradation.
Fresh data loop: new real data arrive every generation, as when re-scraping the web. MAD finds quality and diversity hold with enough fresh real data.

blocks.md: Gerstgrasser et al. studied the accumulate setting in a model simple enough to solve exactly: linear regression. Real data are $y = x \cdot w^* + \epsilon$ with $d$ features and noise variance $\sigma^2$. Each iteration fits ordinary least squares, then relabels the same $T$ inputs using the fitted weights plus fresh noise. Under **replace**, the next fit uses only the newest labels. Under **accumulate**, it uses all labels generated so far, including the original real ones.

blocks.tex: E^{\text{replace}}_{\text{test}} = \frac{\sigma^2 d}{T-d-1}\, n, \qquad E^{\text{accum}}_{\text{test}} = \frac{\sigma^2 d}{T-d-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i^2} \le \frac{\sigma^2 d}{T-d-1} \cdot \frac{\pi^2}{6}
blocks.caption: Test error after n iterations with isotropic features and T at least d + 2 (the replace result is due to Dohmatob, Feng and Kempe, Model Collapse Demystified, as restated in Eq. 4 of Gerstgrasser et al.; the accumulate bound is their Theorem 2)..

blocks.md: Why $1/i^2$? Under accumulation, iteration $i$'s synthetic labels make up a fraction $1/i$ of the training set, so the new noise they inject moves the fit by about $1/i$, and squared error scales that by $1/i^2$. The series $\sum 1/i^2$ converges to $\pi^2/6 \approx 1.645$, so the total error is bounded no matter how many iterations run. Under replacement every iteration contributes a full unit of fresh noise, so errors add up linearly.

blocks.prompt: Take $d = 10$ features, $T = 100$ samples per iteration, $\sigma^2 = 1$. The prefactor is $10/89 = 0.1124$. Predict the test error after 10 iterations under each strategy.
blocks.reveal: **Replace: 1.124**, ten times the first model's error. **Accumulate: 0.174**, since $\sum_{i=1}^{10} 1/i^2 = 1.550$, and it can never exceed $0.1124 \times 1.645 = 0.185$. A 4,000-run simulation of exactly this setup gave 1.108 and 0.172.

blocks.title: Linear regression test error: replace vs accumulate (d = 10, T = 100)

scenes.caption: Iteration 1: both strategies have seen only real data, so both errors are 0.112.
Iteration 2: replace doubles to 0.225; accumulate rises only to 0.140, since the new synthetic labels are half the training set.
Iteration 5: replace 0.562, accumulate 0.165. Each new accumulated batch matters less than the one before.
Iteration 10: replace 1.124 and still growing linearly; accumulate 0.174, under the 0.185 bound it can never cross.

blocks.md: Their language-model experiments agreed: GPT-2 and Llama-2 style models from 9M to about 125M parameters, pretrained from scratch on TinyStories for five iterations, showed rising test loss under replace and flat loss under accumulate. Related theory points the same way. Bertrand et al. prove iterative retraining is stable if the first model is close enough to the data and the share of clean data is large enough. Dohmatob et al. show that mixing even a small fraction of real data eventually ends the scaling plateau of lesson 3.

Accumulation is not a free pass. The bound depends on the original real data never being thrown away, and on synthetic data being added on top rather than diluting a fixed budget: a variant that trains on n times more pure synthetic data still diverges, only more slowly (logarithmically). MAD also reports that a fixed real set only delayed degradation in its image experiments.
The question is not whether synthetic data enter the loop, but whether real data stay in it. Keep the original human data, keep adding fresh real data, and treat synthetic data as an addition.

blocks.question: Under accumulation with d = 10, T = 100 and noise variance 1, what is the test error after iteration 2?
options: 0.225, twice the first iteration
0.112, unchanged
0.185, the bound
0.140, which is 1.25 times the first iteration
blocks.explain: The sum is 1 + 1/4 = 1.25, so the error is 0.1124 x 1.25 = 0.140. Doubling (0.225) is the replace result.

blocks.question: A lab plans each new model's pretraining mix with a fixed 10T-token budget: every year it removes old human text to make room for the latest scrape, which is increasingly model-written. Which strategy from this lesson does that resemble most?
options: Accumulate, because the dataset is being refreshed
Replace, because older real data are discarded and model output takes their place
The fresh data loop, which MAD found safe in all cases
None, because a 10T-token budget is too large for collapse
blocks.explain: Holding the budget fixed while swapping out human text for model output drifts toward the replace setting, where errors compound. Keeping the original real data and growing the corpus matches the accumulate results.

lessons.title: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor

blocks.md: Collapse results describe uncurated loops where a model swallows its own unfiltered output. Successful synthetic data pipelines look different in three ways: they **filter** outputs using a signal that does not come from the generator alone, they **inject diversity** on purpose, and they keep **real data** in the mix. Three well-known papers show each piece.

**Self-Instruct** (Wang et al.) bootstrapped instruction-tuning data from vanilla GPT-3. Starting from 175 human-written seed tasks, the model generates new instructions, inputs and outputs. A new instruction is kept only if its ROUGE-L similarity to every instruction already in the pool is below 0.7, and invalid or similar ones are removed. The run produced about 52K instructions with about 82K instances, and fine-tuning GPT-3 on them gave a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions, on par with InstructGPT-001.

blocks.title: A novelty filter in the style of Self-Instruct (simplified)

scenes.caption: ROUGE-L F1 is based on the longest common subsequence of words: 2 x LCS divided by the total length of both instructions.
A near-duplicate: 5 of its 6 words appear in order in a pool instruction, so the score is 10/11 = 0.91. Rejected.
scenes.output: Write a short poem about rain 0.91 2

scenes.caption: A genuinely new task shares no words in order with the pool: score 0.0. Accepted, so the pool grows to 3.
scenes.output:
Write a short poem about rain 0.91 2
Translate this sentence to French 0.0 3

scenes.caption: Another rephrasing: score 0.83, rejected. Without this filter the model's favorite phrasings would dominate the pool, a small-scale version of tail loss.
scenes.output:
Write a short poem about rain 0.91 2
Translate this sentence to French 0.0 3
Sort a list of numbers in reverse 0.83 3

blocks.md: **phi-1** (Gunasekar et al., *Textbooks Are All You Need*) is a 1.3B-parameter code model trained on about 6B tokens of web code filtered for "educational value" (a classifier trained on GPT-4 annotations), under 1B tokens of GPT-3.5-generated Python textbooks, and about 180M tokens of synthetic exercises for fine-tuning. It reached 50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval and 55.5% on MBPP. The authors stress that naive prompting gives "homogeneous and redundant" data, so they forced diversity by constraining the topics and target audience of each generated textbook.

**STaR** (Zelikman et al., *Self-Taught Reasoner*) makes a model write step-by-step rationales for questions, keeps only rationales that reach the correct answer, retries with the answer given as a hint when it fails, fine-tunes on the kept rationales, and repeats. The filter is a ground-truth label, a signal from outside the model, which is what the uncurated loops in lessons 1 to 4 lacked.

blocks.title: Anatomy of a synthetic data pipeline

scenes.caption: Diversity is injected at the input: varied seeds, topics, audiences or random constraints, because a generator left alone follows its most probable paths.
The filter uses signals the generator does not control: correct answers (STaR), unit tests, a quality classifier (phi-1), or novelty checks (Self-Instruct).
Kept samples join real data rather than replacing it, which is the accumulate setting of lesson 4.
Evaluate on held-out real data, not on synthetic data: a collapsed model can look excellent on its own outputs while losing the tails.

blocks.md: Things to monitor in any synthetic data loop: diversity of the generated set (near-duplicate rate, n-gram or embedding spread), performance on rare slices of a real held-out set, and the share of real data in the mix. Shumailov et al. add a wider point: data known to be human-written, such as pre-LLM crawls, gain value, and provenance tracking matters for anyone training on the web.
Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

blocks.question: A team fine-tunes a model on its own sampled answers to math problems, sampled at temperature 0.3, keeping all of them, for five rounds. Accuracy on their synthetic validation set rises but falls on real exam questions. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The learning rate was too high
No outside signal filters the answers and low temperature narrows the outputs, so each round reinforces the model's own errors and loses rare solution paths
Five rounds is too few for self-training to converge
Math problems cannot benefit from synthetic data
blocks.explain: This is a closed, replacing, tail-cutting loop. STaR-style filtering by correct answers, higher-diversity sampling, and keeping real data in the mix address each part. Validating on synthetic data hid the damage.

blocks.question: Which change most directly addresses the failure that phi-1's authors warned about when prompting a model to write textbooks?
options: Lower the sampling temperature for cleaner text
Generate ten times more textbooks from the same prompt
Vary the topic and target audience in each generation prompt
Train the student for more epochs on the synthetic set
blocks.explain: Their concern was homogeneous, redundant output: a generator repeats its most probable content. Constraining topics and audiences forces coverage. Lower temperature and more samples from one prompt make redundancy worse.
